status.ESTIMATED: no source; `note` carries the one-line justification
status.NOT_FOUND: searched and not located; `note` records where B2 looked

tier.1: regulatory product labeling (openFDA /drug/label, DailyMed SPL) or clinical practice guideline (CPIC)
tier.4: secondary summary — used only where tiers 1-3 failed, and explicitly marked LOW CONFIDENCE

provenance_legend.excipient_reduced_schema: Excipient records use the reduced schema permitted by B1-notes section 1.4. `pk` and `pd` are explicitly null rather than omitted — these substances have no modellable PK/PD. They carry instead: `excipient_function` and `excipient_functions_all`, `excipient_function_provenance` (ESTIMATED for all but magnesium stearate and talc, because the Handbook of Pharmaceutical Excipients and USP-NF <1059> are both paywalled), `max_amount_per_day_mg` (FDA Inactive Ingredient Database regulatory ceiling — a precedent limit, NOT a toxicity threshold), `typical_amount_mg` (NOT_FOUND for every excipient: quantities are trade secret and absent from both label prose and structured SPL), `present_in_products` with a per-product SPL setid citation, `patient_flags` with definitions, `patient_relevance` (HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW) and `formulation_implications` prose.
provenance_legend.salt_handling: Metoprolol is ONE substance record (the moiety) with a `salt_forms` block carrying the tartrate and succinate molecular weights and free-base fractions, and per-formulation PK in `formulations[]`. The PRODUCTS are separate records in data/products.json — metoprolol tartrate IR and metoprolol succinate ER are first-class distinct products with different approved indications. Rationale is in the metoprolol record_notes.

substances.formulation_implications: THE HIGHEST-VALUE PATIENT-LEVEL EXCIPIENT FLAG IN THIS DATASET, and it lands on hydrochlorothiazide. Sunset Yellow is an AZO dye. FDA labelling for products containing FD&C Yellow No. 5 (tartrazine) requires a warning about allergic-type reactions including bronchial asthma, particularly in aspirin-sensitive patients; Yellow No. 6 is in the same chemical class and carries a recognised, if rarer, sensitivity signal. NOTE THE COLLISION WITH THE METOPROLOL ASTHMA CASE: an asthmatic patient can be harmed by the DYE in one product and by the ACTIVE in another. That is a genuinely sophisticated thing for the safety engine to show, and it is only possible because excipients are modelled as first-class substances. Not all HCTZ generics contain it — the ScieGen HCTZ tablet does not — so this is a product-level, not molecule-level, flag. That distinction is the whole argument for the Pills page.
